intro: Unsealed court documents reveal that OpenAI and Microsoft's own employees warned their AI training practices amounted to the "largest theft of labor in human history" — and the "doom loop" they predicted for the web appears to be playing out in real time. Meanwhile, the regulatory landscape is heating up fast, with California's governor pushing for AI kill switches, Virginia creating an AI task force, and a Tasmanian parole board getting caught citing AI-hallucinated case law in a murder case. From geopolitical AI arms races to servers that heat your home, today's roundup covers the full spectrum of where artificial intelligence is reshaping the world.

stories.title: v2.1.278
stories.summary: Version 2.1.278 changes auto mode for Claude API, Enterprise, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, and gateway users to default to a server-side classifier that doesn't charge for classifier overhead. Users can opt out via the CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 environment variable on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, and gateways. It warns when billed fallback occurs. Additionally, a new 'Auto mode server' row was added to the /status command showing whether the session's auto mode classifier is running server-side.
stories.opinion: This is a welcome cost-optimization change. Moving the auto mode classifier server-side and eliminating classifier overhead charges is a meaningful improvement for users on paid infrastructure like Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry where token costs add up quickly. The opt-out mechanism and billed fallback warning show good transparency. The /status integration is a nice touch for debuggability — users can confirm at a glance whether they're getting the server-side benefit. Overall, a practical qual…

stories.title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
stories.summary: The article discusses how Silicon Valley leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, frame China as a major competitive threat in AI development. When asked about slowing AI development due to safety concerns, Trump refused, citing the need to maintain the US lead over China. The piece examines how the 'China bogeyman' narrative is used by American tech firms to argue against AI regulation and safety pauses, suggesting that fears of China surpassing the US in AI serve as a counterweight to concerns about superintelligence risks and are leveraged to justify continued rapid, less-regulated AI development.
stories.opinion: The framing of AI development as a geopolitical race with China creates a false binary between national competitiveness and safety. While genuine strategic competition exists, invoking China as an existential threat to deflect from domestic AI safety concerns is a self-serving argument from companies that profit from minimal regulation. The irony is notable: leaders like Amodei simultaneously warn about AI destroying humanity while arguing we cannot afford to slow down because of China. Thought…

stories.title: Could AI really kill us all? Your questions, answered.
stories.summary: MIT Technology Review hosted a live event asking whether AI could kill humanity. Senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and reporter Grace Huckins answered subscriber questions. They acknowledge real near-term AI risks like autonomous drones, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, and AI-designed pathogens. However, they diverge on existential risk: Huckins notes that AI safety researchers' predictions about capabilities and alignment problems have proved 'disconcertingly accurate,' making her take notice. Heaven is more dismissive of total extinction scenarios, calling them 'apocalyptic science fiction' not grounded in present-day realities, and warns that catastrophizing can distract from immediate problems with AI technology and the companies building it. Both agree the risk of AI causing individual deaths is non-zero, with plausible scenarios including AI-enabled bioweapons and econ…
stories.opinion: The article presents a balanced and accessible treatment of AI existential risk, though it stays fairly surface-level. The most interesting tension is between the two authors: Huckins acknowledges the doomers' track record on predictions while Heaven flatly dismisses extinction scenarios. Heaven's point about catastrophizing distracting from present harms is well-taken but risks becoming its own form of dismissal — the two concerns aren't mutually exclusive. The article would benefit from more…

stories.title: Introducing the Australian Youth Safety Blueprint
stories.summary: OpenAI has introduced the Australian Youth Safety Blueprint, a six-pillar roadmap designed to create safer AI experiences for young people in Australia. The pillars cover AI literacy, age-appropriate safeguards, privacy-protective age assurance, connections to real-world crisis support, and accessible parental controls. The initiative accompanies the rollout of ChatGPT for Teens in Australia, a tailored experience for users aged 13 to 17 with developmental-stage-appropriate safeguards. OpenAI emphasizes that safety responsibility should rest primarily with companies rather than young people or families, and calls for collaboration with educators, researchers, and policymakers to develop evidence-based standards.
stories.opinion: This is a strategically savvy move by OpenAI that serves dual purposes: genuinely advancing youth safety frameworks while also positioning the company favorably in a regulatory environment where Australia has been particularly aggressive on tech regulation affecting minors. The six-pillar approach is substantive in its breadth, but the real test will be in implementation details and independent verification of effectiveness. The framing that companies should bear primary responsibility for safe…

stories.title: India forces caller-ID apps to feed spam reports to telcos
stories.summary: India's telecom regulator TRAI has amended rules to require caller-ID and call-management apps like Truecaller to share users' spam reports with telecom operators via a blockchain-based platform. The move aims to broaden spam enforcement by connecting app-collected reports with telecom industry infrastructure. Truecaller, whose largest market is India with over 350 million users, has called the requirement 'anti-competitive,' arguing it constitutes a one-way transfer of commercially valuable proprietary data to telecom operators. The rules also bar these apps from automatically blocking or spam-tagging calls from certain government-designated number series used for promotional and transactional communications, though individual users can still block such calls on their devices. Technical and jurisdictional questions remain about reporting standards and enforcement against non-telecom co…
stories.opinion: This regulation highlights a genuine tension between centralized spam enforcement and competitive fairness. While pooling spam reports could theoretically improve enforcement against the staggering 42 billion spam calls Indian users faced in 2025, Truecaller's concern about a one-way data transfer is legitimate — the company built its spam detection capabilities through years of investment and community building, and being forced to hand that asset to telecom operators without reciprocity is a…

stories.title: OpenAI and Microsoft knew they were starting a ‘doom loop’ for the web
stories.summary: Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times' lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft reveal internal communications where the companies' own employees warned that their AI training practices constituted the 'largest theft of labor in human history,' would create a 'doom loop' damaging the web, and made a 'complete mockery of fair use.' Key quotes came from Microsoft's Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht, though Microsoft has tried to distance itself from his views, calling them one employee's individual perspective. The article notes that the predicted 'Google Zero' scenario — where AI replaces web traffic — has largely come true.
stories.opinion: These revelations are significant because they show that the companies were not merely unaware of potential harms but had internal voices explicitly warning about them. Microsoft's attempt to characterize Hecht as an intentional contrarian doesn't fully absolve the company — employing someone specifically to raise these concerns and then proceeding anyway arguably demonstrates informed disregard rather than ignorance. The fact that the predicted 'doom loop' of declining web traffic has material…

stories.title: v2.1.275
stories.summary: Version 2.1.275 adds four features: signed-in account confirmation and display during gateway sign-in, a ctrl+enter send-now key that interrupts the current turn to send queued messages immediately, a startup warning when an OpenTelemetry headers helper fails silently, and syncing of skills across sessions.
stories.opinion: This is a solid quality-of-life release. The send-now key (ctrl+enter) is the standout addition — being able to interrupt a turn and flush queued messages addresses a real friction point in interactive workflows where you realize mid-generation that you need to redirect. The gateway account confirmation is a sensible security hygiene improvement that prevents credential confusion. The otelHeadersHelper warning is a small but valuable observability fix; silent telemetry failures are notoriously…

stories.title: Domestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your home
stories.summary: The article discusses an innovative approach to home heating where compact computer servers (domestic datacentres) are attached to hot water cylinders in homes. These servers generate heat as a byproduct of their computing operations and transfer that heat to warm household water, replacing traditional gas heating. The piece profiles Giles Gibson in London who uses this setup, and frames it as a money-saving alternative as energy bills are scheduled to rise. The concept essentially repurposes waste heat from data processing into useful domestic heating.
stories.opinion: This is a genuinely clever application of thermodynamics — data processing inevitably produces heat, and routing that waste heat into something useful rather than venting it is elegant engineering. The economics could be compelling if the computing revenue offsets electricity costs while also displacing gas heating bills. However, I'd want to understand the practical details better: noise levels, maintenance burden, what happens when the computing workload drops and you still need hot water, an…

stories.title: Tilly Norwood’s press tour is going about as well as you’d expect for an AI
stories.summary: Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated 'actress' created by Particle6 Group, is having a disastrous press tour promoting its upcoming film 'Misaligned.' During 75 simultaneous journalist interviews, the AI made numerous errors, most notably in a recorded interview with Piers Morgan and actor Tom Conti where it abruptly malfunctioned and began speaking Chinese mid-sentence. When questioned, it apologized for the 'hiccup' and referenced 'wires getting crossed.' The article speculates that Particle6 may have intentionally made the AI perform poorly to generate viral attention, since people would be more likely to talk about Norwood if they were making fun of it.
stories.opinion: This story highlights the uncanny valley problem that persists even as AI technology advances rapidly. Tilly Norwood's glitchy press tour — whether genuinely broken or strategically orchestrated — underscores how far we are from AI convincingly replacing human performers in unscripted, real-time social interactions. The incident also raises interesting questions about AI marketing strategy: if Particle6 deliberately made Norwood fail publicly, it's a cynical but possibly effective ploy to gener…

stories.title: Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centers
stories.summary: Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22, which bans executive branch officials from signing NDAs for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and mandates a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers. The order also establishes an AI task force to evaluate how the state government can address risks like workforce displacement and data privacy, and how existing law can apply to AI harms. This follows a broader trend of states taking data center and AI policy into their own hands, with California, New York, and Texas governors also taking similar executive actions, as Congress and President Trump have been slow to act on sweeping changes.
stories.opinion: This is a pragmatic and balanced move by Governor Spanberger. Banning NDAs for data center projects is a particularly strong transparency measure — communities deserve to know what's being built in their backyards and what resources those facilities will consume. The AI task force focused on workforce displacement and data privacy addresses real, immediate concerns rather than speculative sci-fi scenarios. The broader trend of states stepping in where federal action has stalled is notable: it c…

stories.title: v2.1.276
stories.summary: Version 2.1.276 of Claude Code fixes a regression introduced in v2.1.275 where every API request would fail with a 400 error mentioning 'Input tag advisor_20260301' when the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL environment variable was configured to point at a proxy or gateway instead of the default Anthropic API endpoint.
stories.opinion: This is a critical hotfix release addressing a breaking regression that would have blocked all users relying on proxies or API gateways — a common setup in enterprise and team environments. The fast turnaround from 2.1.275 to 2.1.276 suggests good incident response. The root cause appears to be that v2.1.275 started sending an internal/beta API tag ('advisor_20260301') that the official Anthropic API silently accepts but third-party proxies and gateways reject as invalid input. This is a good r…

stories.title: Tasmanian justice department review under way after AI and fake citation used in murderer’s parole decision
stories.summary: Tasmania's justice department is conducting a review after a parole board cited non-existent case law — likely generated by AI — in setting conditions for convicted murderer Susan Neill-Fraser. The fabricated legal citation led to a parole condition being deemed invalid, prompting broader scrutiny of potential AI use in the state's parole decision-making processes.
stories.opinion: This case illustrates one of the most dangerous failure modes of large language models: hallucinated citations presented with false confidence in high-stakes legal settings. When AI-generated text containing fabricated case law makes its way into binding parole decisions, it undermines both the rights of the individual subject to those conditions and public trust in the justice system. The core problem isn't that someone used AI — it's that the output wasn't verified against actual legal databa…

stories.title: A startup that builds other startups raised $100M and is all-in on physical AI
stories.summary: UP.Labs, now rebranded as Vantora, has raised $100 million from Silversmith Capital Partners to continue its model of building startups on behalf of large corporate partners like Porsche, Alaska Airlines, J.B. Hunt, and others. The key strategic shift is that Vantora is now focused on building startups exclusively for its corporate customers rather than the broader market, creating a 'proprietary M&A pipeline' where partners can fold the startups into their core businesses. This change has unlocked bigger opportunities in physical AI — areas like retrofitting industrial hardware for autonomy — that were previously too sensitive or strategically important for corporations to let a third party commercialize externally.
stories.opinion: This is a genuinely interesting business model evolution. The original UP.Labs concept of building startups for corporates was clever but had an inherent tension: the most valuable problems were exactly the ones corporations wouldn't let you sell externally. By pivoting to a proprietary model where the corporate partner can acquire the startup, Vantora resolves that tension and gains access to higher-value, more defensible opportunities. The physical AI angle is smart timing — large industrials…

stories.title: Gavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch
stories.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order positioning the state to lead on AI oversight. The order convenes an expert group to deliver recommendations within two months on strengthening AI safety measures in state law. Key proposals include mandating a 'kill switch' for frontier AI models that is routinely verified as effective, requiring AI companies to embed independent verification groups onsite for regular audits, making transparency reports and risk assessments subject to independent auditor standards, and requiring companies to report 'loss-of-control incidents' as critical safety incidents. The order also directs a state agency to accelerate implementation of two recent laws creating a framework for independent AI safety verifiers and a state registry of AI auditors. This move comes as Congress remains unlikely to pass substantive AI legislation before the midter…
stories.opinion: Newsom's executive order represents a pragmatic move to fill the federal regulatory vacuum on AI safety. The specific proposals—kill switches, onsite auditors, mandatory incident reporting—are concrete and actionable rather than vague aspirational language, which is encouraging. However, the effectiveness will depend entirely on implementation details: a 'kill switch' for a frontier model is technically complex and could be rendered meaningless if poorly defined, and the two-month timeline for…
